title: Piano Sonata No. 21 in C major, “Waldstein”
hook: A sonata that starts with a quiet pulse and ends in a blaze of light, often heard as a sunrise.

painting.title: Sun Rising through Vapour
painting.pairingNote: Painted within three years of the sonata, a pale sun breaking through morning mist over a glassy sea; in Italy the sonata is known as “L’Aurora”, the dawn, for the way the finale’s theme glows out of the haze of the pedal.

facts: Beethoven sketched the sonata in late 1803, just before starting work on his opera *Fidelio*, and finished it in 1804. In August 1804 he offered it to the publisher Breitkopf & Härtel together with the sonatas Op. 54 and the *Appassionata*. It belongs to the years of the *Eroica* Symphony, when his music grew bigger and bolder.

It is dedicated to Count Ferdinand von Waldstein, one of his first patrons in Bonn. When the young Beethoven left Bonn for Vienna in 1792, Waldstein wrote in his album: “receive Mozart’s spirit from Haydn’s hands”. It is the only work Beethoven dedicated to him, though by 1804 the two seem to have had little contact.

Beethoven first wrote a long, gentle slow movement. According to his pupil Ferdinand Ries, a friend said the sonata was too long; Beethoven was furious, then agreed. He replaced it with a short *Introduzione* and published the original separately as the *Andante favori*.

The sonata asks a great deal of the pianist and of the instrument: rumbling repeated chords, long trills, runs in both hands and, in the last minutes, scales in octaves marked to be played as glissandos. Many writers have heard it as orchestral, almost a concerto without orchestra.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a quiet engine starts and builds (I), a dark, hushed doorway (II), a sunrise and a dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro con brio
movements.summary: The sonata begins with no tune at all, only soft chords repeated low on the piano, like an engine starting. Out of that pulse grows a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] of great energy. The contrast comes from a calm, hymn-like second theme in an unexpected key.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: quick, quiet repeated chords in the low-middle register, with short answering flicks high up.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a slow, hymn-like tune in chords, marked *dolce e molto legato*, in E major.

stops.hear: Soft, quick chords hammered low and evenly, then little phrases high above; the pattern restarts a step lower
stops.happening: Theme 1. No melody yet, only rhythm and harmony

stops.hear: The opening again, now shimmering: the chords become a fast, trembling flutter
Everything calms: a slow, quiet tune in chords, like a hymn
stops.happening: Theme 2, in E major, a bright and distant key

stops.hear: The hymn breaks into rising triplet runs, louder and faster
stops.happening: The music builds towards the end of the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The opening rhythm returns in a new key and starts to wander
A long, rumbling build in the bass, getting louder, then a sudden hush
The soft, repeated chords from the start
The music stops on two long held chords, as if listening
The hymn tune, now in A major
The repeated chords start again in a soft, far-off key
The hymn returns gently in C major, then slows almost to a stop

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A loud final rush up the keyboard and hard closing chords

notice: Listen to the very start. For two bars there is no tune, only a pulse of chords. Beethoven builds the whole movement on rhythm first.
Compare the hymn’s two appearances: in E major in the first half, in A major after the return. The same tune seems to change colour with the key.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Kempff recorded the sonata in September 1964 in the Beethovensaal in Hanover, for his stereo cycle of all 32 sonatas. He does not take the repeat of the exposition, so the first movement lasts about eight and a half minutes; pianists who repeat it, Pollini among them, take about ten.

movements.heading: Introduzione. Adagio molto
movements.summary: A short, dark, very quiet slow movement that sounds like the door to the finale rather than a movement of its own. Deep chords and a hesitant rhythm wander through distant keys; a brief singing line appears, and the music sinks onto a long-held note that leads straight into the rondo.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: deep, soft chords with a short, dotted figure, moving through strange harmonies.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a brief, singing melody in the middle of the keyboard.

stops.hear: Very soft, deep octaves and chords, with a short dotted lift; the harmony drifts into unexpected places
Calmer chords in F, then a singing line in the middle register
The deep opening chords return
Under a slow line in the right hand, the left hand ripples in fast notes
stops.happening: The rhythm quickens, a hint of what is coming

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Soft chords settle on a long note and fade, without an ending
stops.happening: The music waits on the threshold; the rondo follows at once

notice: Notice that the movement never really ends. It stops on a held note that leads, without a pause, into the finale.

movements.heading: Rondo. Allegretto moderato – Prestissimo
movements.summary: Out of the hush, a simple, glowing tune rises in the middle of the piano, held in a haze of pedal. This is the “dawn” of the Italian nickname. The tune returns again and again in a [[rondo|rondo]], growing to full brilliance, and the movement ends in a breathless *Prestissimo*.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow-moving, folk-like tune, played by the left hand crossing over the right, over a low bass note that keeps ringing.

mainIdeas.name: The stormy episodes
mainIdeas.description: driving triplets, a fierce passage in A minor, and a central section in C minor built on hammered octaves.

mainIdeas.name: The *Prestissimo*
mainIdeas.description: the theme sped up, with scales in octaves and a long trill.

stops.hear: Very soft: a simple tune in the middle of the keyboard over a deep, ringing bass, the sound blurred by the pedal
stops.happening: The rondo theme, in C major. Beethoven asks for long [[sustain-pedal|sustain pedal]]

stops.hear: The tune again, now loud and bright, with a long [[trill|trill]] above it and fast scales below
Rolling triplets, then a stormy, insistent passage in a minor key
stops.happening: The first episode, turning to A minor

stops.hear: The glowing tune returns softly
stops.happening: The first return of the theme

stops.hear: Loud, hammered octaves in C minor; swirling notes in threes take over
The tune in loud chords, moved through new keys, then broken into pieces
A long, quiet passage of floating, rippling chords
The tune bursts out loud in C major
Big chords, then the music fades almost to nothing, as if the movement were dying away
Suddenly very fast and light: the tune in quick notes
Quiet scales sweep down and up in octaves
stops.happening: The octaves Beethoven marks to be played as a [[glissando|glissando]]

stops.hear: The tune high above, held on a long trill, with quick notes below
stops.happening: Theme, trill and accompaniment all in two hands

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Loud, rushing runs and final chords

notice: Listen to the haze in the first minute. Beethoven marks long stretches with the pedal held down, so the harmonies blur into each other like light through mist.
In the *Prestissimo*, listen for the moment the hands seem to slide along the keyboard. These are the octave glissandos, passed between the two hands.

threads.title: Pulse before melody
threads.body: The first movement starts with rhythm alone; the finale’s theme grows out of a held haze. Beethoven makes sound and motion as important as tunes.

threads.title: Bright, distant keys
threads.body: The hymn of the first movement appears in E major and A major, far from home, which is why it sounds so luminous.

threads.title: An orchestra in one piano
threads.body: Rumbling repeated chords, long trills, and runs in both hands at once: the sonata treats the piano as an orchestra.
